global: **Who published the CVE matters most, then the vendor's KEV history, then CVSS.** Mean |SHAP| on 2,000 random test CVEs is 0.79 log-odds for **CNA**, 0.65 for **vendor KEV entries (all time)**, 0.41 for **CNA CVSS score**, 0.36 for description length and 0.35 for CVSS 'privileges required'. For **exploited** CVEs, vendor KEV history is the biggest mover (1.14), ahead of CNA (0.90) and CVSS score (0.66). By group: who (vendor/CNA/CWE) 1.40, CVSS 1.39, KEV history 0.91, text-derived 0.36. The day-0 exploitation phrase is ~0 on random CVEs because almost none have one. It is decisive for the few that do, which is the Apple pattern from Phase 3. 'vendor has any KEV entry' and 'has CNA CVSS' add nothing beyond the other features.
beeswarm: **Many earlier KEV entries for the vendor (red) push scores up by up to +2.5 log-odds; none (blue) pull them down by about −0.4.** High CNA CVSS pushes up and low CVSS pushes down, but the spread is smaller than for KEV history. **A recent KEV entry for the vendor (few days since, blue) pushes up by up to +1.2.** CNA and CWE spread widely in both directions: some publishers raise scores (VulnCheck +1.6 on average; Google Chrome, Oracle, Microsoft, MITRE about +0.6), while the WordPress-plugin CNAs lower them (Wordfence −1.6, WPScan −1.5, Patchstack −1.4). Longer descriptions tend to push up mildly. The model mostly reads **who is affected and whether attackers already target that vendor**, then how severe the bug is.
examples: **Caught: CVE-2026-24858 (Fortinet FortiWeb/FortiAnalyzer authentication bypass, CVSS 9.8).** It ranked #1 in its month. The drivers are CVSS 9.8 (+1.6), CWE-288 authentication bypass (+1.1), Fortinet's 24 earlier KEV entries (+1.1), a long detailed description (+1.0) and the Fortinet PSIRT as publisher (+0.7). CISA listed it in KEV the same day. **Missed: CVE-2026-56155 (Microsoft AD FS privilege escalation, CVSS 7.8, local).** Microsoft's ~364 KEV entries push it up strongly (+2.4), but it is a local, authenticated privilege escalation with a 7.8 score. It landed in the top 6.4% of a ~9,000-CVE month, outside the top 110. This is the 2026 drift in one CVE: dozens of Microsoft CVEs a month get the same KEV-history push, and a fixed 110 slots can't hold them all. **False alarm: CVE-2026-20079 (Cisco FMC unauthenticated auth bypass to root, CVSS 10.0).** It looks exactly like an exploited CVE: CVSS 10 (+1.5), Cisco's ~89 KEV entries (+1.5), CWE-288 (+1.3). It *was* added to KEV, **189 days after publication**, so it counts as 'not exploited' only because of the 90-day label window. This is not typical but not rare at the top: **3% of the non-exploited CVEs in the monthly top 10** (5 of 164) and 0.8% in the top 110 (16 of 2,100) were later added to KEV, vs 0.05% of all non-exploited CVEs. Some 'false alarms' are exploits that came late.
kev_year: **KEV history pushes more non-exploited CVEs up in 2026.** For exploited CVEs the push is unchanged (mean +1.06 in 2025, +1.04 in 2026). For non-exploited random CVEs it rose from **0.00 to +0.23** on average, and the share of non-exploited CVEs with a KEV push above +1 log-odds rose from **18.8% to 26.6%**. The group's share of all SHAP mass went from 21.0% to 23.5%. The signal didn't get weaker for exploited CVEs; it now applies to many more CVEs that aren't exploited. That is the mechanism behind the 2026 drop in notebook 06: more look-alikes compete for the same 110 slots.
same_capacity: Over the test period there are about **176 exploited CVEs a year**. At **110 patches a month**, gradient boosting catches **~59 a year**, vs ~44 for the best day-0 rule (**+15 a year**) and ~33 for CVSS ranking (**+27 a year**). At the **CVSS ≥ 9 rule's own capacity (385 a month)** it catches **+19 exploited CVEs a year** (51.7% vs 41.2%). Against 'phrase OR CVSS ≥ 9' (387 a month) the gain is **+8 a year** (51.7% vs 47.3%).
same_recall: **Over the whole test period, gradient boosting matches the CVSS ≥ 9 rule's 41% recall with 198 patches a month instead of 385.** That saves **187 patches a month, ~13,500 analyst hours and ~$1.35M a year** at 6 h per patch and $100/h. Against 'phrase OR CVSS ≥ 9' it needs 265 instead of 387 (122 fewer a month, ~8,750 h, ~$0.9M). **The saving is concentrated in 2025** (83 vs 238 patches). **In 2026 the frozen model barely saves anything** (569 vs 606 against CVSS ≥ 9), **and it needs more patches than 'phrase OR CVSS ≥ 9'** (630 vs 607). **A quarterly-retrained model restores the advantage in 2026: 302 patches vs 606** (about half). The saving is real but needs a maintained model.
ransomware: On the **43 ransomware-linked exploited CVEs**, gradient boosting catches **42.2% [27–57] at 110 a month**, vs **27.9%** for EPSS, **26.7%** for the best rule and **24.6%** for CVSS ranking. At 385 a month it catches 65.1% vs the CVSS ≥ 9 rule's 58.1% (25 of 43); the fusion reaches 74.4% at 385. The model does *better* on ransomware-linked CVEs than on the rest (42.2% vs 32.2%), probably because ransomware groups favour edge devices and enterprise software from vendors with long KEV histories. The CIs are wide (43 CVEs), so read this as 'at least as good on the most damaging CVEs', not as a precise gain.
policy: **Capacity is the bigger lever; retraining is the second.** Scaling the budget with volume (4.22% of each month, 127–412 patches a month in test, avg 216) raises the frozen model from 33.7% to **42.5%**. Scaling plus quarterly retraining reaches **46.9%**: **44.4% in 2026** (vs 23.9% at frozen K = 110) and 49.1% in 2025. A fixed K spending the same total patches does about as well (41.8% / 48.0%). So the gain comes from **keeping capacity in line with CVE volume**, not from the share rule itself. Cost: an average of +106 patches a month over 110, about **+7,700 analyst hours a year** (+12,700 at the 2026 rate). Retraining alone at K = 110 is break-even overall (+1.0) but +7.4 points in 2026.
ciso: **Recommendation: replace 'patch everything with CVSS ≥ 9' with a model-ranked emergency list, retrained every quarter, with capacity reviewed against CVE volume.** On 20 months of unseen data (2025-01 → 2026-08, 294 exploited CVEs), the model caught **33.7% of exploited CVEs with 110 emergency patches a month**, vs 25.2% for the best rule a careful team could run today and 18.6% for CVSS ranking. That is **+15 to +27 more exploited CVEs patched early each year at the same workload**. At the CVSS ≥ 9 rule's own workload (385 patches a month) it catches 51.7% vs 41.2%. To match that rule's coverage it needs **198 patches a month instead of 385, about 13,500 analyst hours (~$1.35M) a year at our assumptions**. On **ransomware-linked** CVEs it catches 42% vs 25–28% for the rules and EPSS. **Against EPSS**, the industry score, the model is ahead overall (33.7% vs 29.6%, not statistically clear). **But 37% of all exploited CVEs (109 of 294) were already in CISA's KEV list when EPSS produced the score used**, and EPSS is assumed to use KEV. On CVEs not yet in KEV, the model catches **30.4% vs 14.6%** for EPSS. **Caveat: with very small capacity (≤ 50 patches a month), EPSS ranks its very top slightly better**, and EPSS needs a day longer (only 30% of CVEs have an EPSS score on publication day). **The risk is drift**: in 2026 CVE volume rose 70% and many more CVEs came from vendors already in KEV. The frozen model fell to 23.9% at a fixed 110 patches, and lost its workload advantage. **Retraining each quarter (31.3% in 2026) and sizing capacity to ~4% of each month's CVEs (44% in 2026 with retraining)** recover most of the loss. Budget about 7,700 extra hours a year at today's volumes for the larger patch list, or accept lower coverage at 110. Explanations are available for every ranked CVE: vendor's exploitation history, publisher, severity and bug type.
